lead: This unit explains how electrical quantities are measured, how electric power is generated and delivered, and how homes are wired safely. After it, you can choose a meter or sensor, read a tariff bill, size a fuse or MCB, and estimate a rooftop solar plant.
about: This unit connects measurement, power supply and safety in one line. Chapter 6.1 explains moving-coil and moving-iron meters, and 6.2 extends the idea to energy meters, meggers, digital multimeters and oscilloscopes. Chapter 6.3 shows how sensors turn physical quantities into signals. Chapters 6.4 and 6.5 follow electric power from coal, nuclear, solar and wind sources through generation, transmission and an 11 kV/400 V substation. Chapter 6.6 uses meter readings for tariff, energy audit and rooftop solar. Chapters 6.7 and 6.8 cover residential wiring, fuses, circuit breakers, residual-current devices and earthing. Each chapter uses earlier circuit and machine ideas, and every calculation keeps units visible.

chapters.idea: A moving-coil meter deflects in proportion to current, while a moving-iron meter deflects in proportion to current squared, so one suits DC and the other also works on AC.
chapters.depth: Construction and torque for permanent-magnet moving-coil (PMMC) and moving-iron attraction and repulsion types. Deflection: θ ∝ I for PMMC, θ ∝ I² for moving iron. Spring control, air or oil damping, bearings and pointer. Shunt and series multiplier for range extension. Moving iron reads RMS on AC and has a non-uniform scale; PMMC reads average DC and needs a rectifier for AC. Some syllabi call PMMC a D'Arsonval meter. Include advantages, errors and typical uses.

figure.aria: A straight line shows moving-coil deflection rising linearly with current; a curve shows moving-iron deflection rising as current squared, using a 5 A full scale.

chapters.example: Two ammeters have the same full-scale current of 5 A: a moving-coil meter with θ ∝ I and a moving-iron meter with θ ∝ I². Find the deflection as a fraction of full scale at 2 A for each. Answer: moving coil 0.4 or 40%; moving iron 0.16 or 16%.
chapters.trap: The moving-iron scale is crowded at the low end and reads RMS on AC. A PMMC meter on AC without a rectifier reads zero or a wrong value because it responds to average torque.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 current and voltage; Unit 2 RMS value and phasors for AC deflection.
chapters.leave: AC power, phasors and three-phase quantities to Unit 2; magnetic circuits and machine torque to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Each instrument measures a different electrical quantity: an energy meter counts kWh, a megger tests insulation resistance, a DMM measures V, I and R, and a DSO shows waveforms.
chapters.depth: Induction energy meter: voltage coil, current coil, rotating aluminium disc, brake magnet and register; meter constant in revolutions per kWh. Megger: hand or battery high-voltage DC source and ohm scale for insulation resistance; never on live circuits. Digital multimeter: ADC, input impedance, auto-ranging, continuity and diode test. DSO: attenuator, ADC, memory, trigger and time base; probe ground and safety. Some syllabi call the megger an insulation resistance tester. Include reading scales and common errors.

figure.title: Induction energy meter
figure.aria: Voltage and current coils drive an aluminium disc; a brake magnet controls its speed and a register counts the revolutions as energy.

chapters.example: A single-phase energy meter supplies 230 V, 5 A at power factor 0.8 for 6 hours. Find the energy in kWh and the cost at ₹8.00 per unit. Answer: power = 230 × 5 × 0.8 = 920 W; energy = 0.92 × 6 = 5.52 kWh; cost = 5.52 × 8 = ₹44.16.
chapters.trap: Energy is kWh, not kW; a megger uses high DC voltage and is unsafe on live circuits; a DSO ground clip is not a floating input.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1 for meter deflection; Unit 2 for power factor and RMS.
chapters.leave: Tariff calculation to 6.6; sensor signal details to 6.3; ADC architecture to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A transducer converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal; the Hall effect uses a magnetic field, and a proximity sensor detects an object without contact.
chapters.depth: Definition of sensor and transducer; active and passive; analog and digital output. Hall effect: current I through a thin semiconductor in magnetic field B gives transverse voltage V_H = K_H I B; sign reverses with B or I; used for speed, position and current sensing. Proximity sensors: inductive (metal only), capacitive (metal and dielectric), optical; range, hysteresis and NPN/PNP output. Signal conditioning with amplifier and comparator. Some syllabi call a Hall sensor a magnetic sensor. Include applications in motor speed and phone flip cover.

figure.title: Hall sensor signal chain
figure.aria: A constant current and a magnetic field act on a Hall element; its small Hall voltage is amplified and compared with a threshold to give a switch output.

chapters.example: A Hall sensor has sensitivity 20 V/(A·T). It carries 10 mA in a field of 0.2 T. Find the Hall voltage. If the amplifier gain is 100, find the output. Answer: V_H = 20 × 0.01 × 0.2 = 0.04 V = 40 mV; output = 4 V.
chapters.trap: Hall voltage is small and reverses with field direction; inductive proximity sensors detect only metals, while capacitive types can detect non-metals; check range and hysteresis.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 op-amp comparator for threshold; Unit 3 magnetic field ideas.
chapters.leave: Detailed op-amp circuits to Unit 4; microcontroller interfacing to Unit 5; power-system sensors to 6.5.

chapters.idea: Electric power comes from non-renewable sources such as coal thermal and nuclear, and renewable sources such as solar and wind.
chapters.depth: Block flow of a coal thermal plant: coal, boiler, steam, turbine, generator, condenser. Nuclear: fission heat, primary coolant, steam, turbine. Solar: photovoltaic cell, module, array; irradiance and temperature. Wind: turbine, gearbox, generator; cut-in and rated speed. Comparison: capital cost, fuel cost, availability, emissions and land. Some syllabi call non-renewable sources conventional and renewable sources non-conventional. Include Indian examples such as coal, solar and wind, but no exact capacity figures.

figure.aria: A tree splits electric power sources into non-renewable coal thermal and nuclear, and renewable solar, wind, hydro and biomass.

chapters.example: A coal thermal plant has overall efficiency 35%. Coal calorific value is 25 MJ/kg. Find coal needed per kWh generated. Answer: 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ; input = 3.6 / 0.35 = 10.29 MJ; coal = 10.29 / 25 = 0.412 kg.
chapters.trap: Capacity in MW is not energy in MWh; nuclear is not renewable; solar and wind output depends on weather and is rated at standard conditions.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 synchronous generator for mechanical-to-electrical conversion; Unit 2 AC generation.
chapters.leave: Transmission and distribution to 6.5; tariff and solar sizing to 6.6; power electronics to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Power flows from generation at 11-25 kV, is stepped up for transmission, stepped down at substations, and reaches homes at 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase.
chapters.depth: Simple layout: generator, step-up transformer, transmission line, step-down substations, primary distribution, 11 kV/400 V distribution transformer and consumer. Why high voltage reduces line loss: P_loss = I²R, and P = √3 V I cosφ. 11 kV/400 V substation: incoming 11 kV bus, transformer, LT bus, feeders and protection. Star and delta windings, line and phase voltages. Some syllabi call the final transformer a distribution transformer. Include reading a single-line diagram.

figure.title: Generation to consumer
figure.aria: A generator feeds a step-up transformer, a high-voltage transmission line, step-down substations, an 11 kV feeder and a local 11 kV/400 V transformer before the consumer.

chapters.example: An 11 kV/400 V, 100 kVA distribution transformer supplies a balanced load at 0.8 power factor. Find the line currents on the 11 kV and 400 V sides. Answer: I_LV = 100000 / (√3 × 400) = 144.3 A; I_HV = 100000 / (√3 × 11000) = 5.25 A.
chapters.trap: 400 V is line voltage and 230 V is phase voltage in a three-phase four-wire system; high voltage lowers current and loss but needs more insulation and clearance.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 three-phase star/delta and line/phase values; Unit 3 transformer principle.
chapters.leave: Transformer equivalent circuit and protection coordination to later courses; tariff to 6.6; wiring to 6.7.

chapters.idea: The tariff turns meter units into a bill; an energy audit finds waste; a rooftop solar plant is sized from monthly kWh and can use net metering.
chapters.depth: Tariff: fixed charge, energy charge, slabs, power factor penalty and fuel surcharge; one unit is 1 kWh. Energy audit: list loads, measure kWh, find high-use items and estimate savings. Rooftop solar: daily kWh = kW × peak sun hours × performance ratio; panel count = array kW / panel kW; inverter size; subsidy and net metering: bill on import minus export. Some syllabi call net metering net billing loosely. Include payback = net cost / monthly saving.

figure.title: Rooftop solar and net metering
figure.aria: Solar panels feed an inverter and a net meter; the meter supplies home loads and can export surplus to the grid or import a deficit.

chapters.example: A home uses 300 kWh per month. It plans a 3 kW rooftop system using 500 W panels. Average generation is 4 kWh per kW per day for 30 days. Find the panel count, monthly generation and simple payback. Cost is ₹60,000 per kW, subsidy is ₹15,000 per kW, saved energy is valued at ₹7 per kWh for 300 kWh per month, and export credit is ignored. Answer: 6 panels; 360 kWh per month; net cost ₹1,35,000; saving ₹2,100 per month; payback 64.3 months.
chapters.trap: kW is power and kWh is energy; subsidy may be capped by kW; net metering credits only grid-tied systems and billing is on net import, not total generation.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.2 energy meter reading; Chapter 6.4 solar source; Chapter 6.5 distribution and meter.
chapters.leave: Detailed tariff law to later; inverter design to power electronics; wiring to 6.7.

chapters.idea: Residential wiring brings live, neutral and earth to circuits protected by fuses or MCBs, with an RCCB or ELCB for shock protection.
chapters.depth: Service entrance, meter, main switch, distribution board and sub-circuits for lights, sockets, geyser and AC. Wire colour code: live brown or red, neutral blue or black, earth green or yellow-green; some syllabi use old colours. Fuse: rewirable or HRC, melts on overcurrent. MCB: thermal-magnetic, resettable. RCCB or ELCB: detects residual current to earth and does not protect against overload. Load calculation, diversity, cable size and MCB rating. Some syllabi call RCCB an RCD.

figure.title: Residential distribution board
figure.aria: Service enters through an energy meter and main switch to an RCCB, then an MCB board splits into light and power circuits.

chapters.example: A 230 V residential circuit supplies a 2 kW geyser. Find the current. Choose a standard MCB rating at least 25% above the current from 6 A, 10 A, 16 A and 20 A. Answer: I = 2000 / 230 = 8.70 A; 1.25 × 8.70 = 10.87 A; choose 16 A.
chapters.trap: A fuse or MCB protects wiring from overload and short circuit, not people from electric shock; an RCCB protects people. Never put the earth wire through a fuse or switch.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 Ohm's law and power; Chapter 6.6 load and bill; Chapter 6.2 energy meter.
chapters.leave: Earthing types and electrode resistance to 6.8; detailed wiring rules to later.

chapters.idea: Earthing connects exposed metal to the soil so a fault current flows and the protective device trips, while the body stays near earth potential.
chapters.depth: Need: safety of persons and equipment, voltage stabilisation, and a path for lightning and surge currents. Types: plate, pipe, rod, strip and mesh; maintenance-free chemical earthing. Working: earth wire from the body to the electrode; earth resistance R_e; fault current I_f ≈ V/R_e; touch voltage. Good earth resistance is low and is measured by an earth tester or megger. Some syllabi call earthing grounding. Include dos and don'ts: never use neutral as earth, keep joints tight and water the pit.

figure.title: Fault path through earthing
figure.aria: A live-to-body fault sends current through the earth wire and electrode into the soil; the large fault current trips the fuse or MCB.

chapters.example: A 230 V metal-bodied appliance has a fault from live to body. The earth wire and electrode have total resistance 5 Ω. Find the fault current. Will a 16 A MCB see this as a large fault? Answer: I_f = 230 / 5 = 46 A; yes.
chapters.trap: Earthing does not absorb current; it gives a low-resistance return so the fuse or MCB trips. A high earth resistance keeps fault current low and may not trip, so an RCCB is added.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.7 safety devices; Unit 1 Ohm's law; Chapter 6.2 megger.
chapters.leave: Lightning protection and substation earthing design to later; detailed wiring to 6.7.
